claims.claim: Epiphanius was bishop of Salamis (Constantia), the metropolis of the island of Cyprus.
Epiphanius was born c. 315 near Eleutheropolis, Palestine, and died in 403 at sea on his return journey from Constantinople to Cyprus.
Epiphanius was elected bishop of Salamis in 367 and fulfilled the duties of the episcopate for nearly forty years.

A small corpus of writings against images attributed to Epiphanius includes three long texts: the letters to the emperor Theodosius and to John bishop of Jerusalem and the so-called Tractatus contra eos qui imagines faciunt.

The iconophobic fragments attributed to Epiphanius are preserved mainly within sources tied to the Iconoclastic Controversy, except for the letter to John of Jerusalem, which was translated into Latin by Jerome.
The authenticity of the iconophobic writings attributed to Epiphanius is disputed and has been the subject of extensive scholarly debate since their first modern publication in 1916.
John of Damascus argued that the work rejecting images attributed to Epiphanius was fictitious and unauthentic.
The letter to John of Jerusalem, which includes the account of Epiphanius tearing down a curtain with an image in a church at Anablatha, is accepted as authentic by modern scholars.

In the letter to John of Jerusalem, dated c. 394, Epiphanius urged the bishop to be careful of the offence of images in churches and described tearing down a curtain with an image of Christ or a saint.

The letter to Emperor Theodosius argues against painting images of Christ and the apostles, claiming that such practices were not done by the ancient fathers and that artists lie by representing saints in different forms.

The iconophobic documents attributed to Epiphanius have been used to prove a stream of iconoclasm already in the fourth and fifth centuries, and the Iconoclasts of the eighth and ninth centuries quoted them as evidence for their position.
